No worries, it is a hard one to picture. Here is the plain version.

The hardest part of a quantum computer is reading its own mistakes fast enough. That part just got a lot cheaper.

A quantum computer writes with a leaky pen. Every line comes out smudged, and you cannot stop it from smudging. What you can do is read the page fast enough to know what it meant to write.

That reading has to keep up. The machine hands over a page every few milliseconds, and an ordinary computer has to read each one before the next lands. Fall behind and the machine stops and waits.

Walking Cat is the architecture IonQ published in April. Ions move around the chip, and cat states are used to check the writing without touching the page itself. So the page comes back in the same shape every time, which is why one reader can keep up.

Measured this week: that reading fits on 12 cores of a laptop processor, for a simulated machine of 408 logical qubits. The delay adds under 0.3% to the computation time.

Until now that job was expected to need racks of dedicated chips. That is the part that changed.

$IONQ IonQ is no longer just a quantum computing company it’s building the global infrastructure for our quantum future

Mihir Bhaskar, SVP R&D, keynote at the Optica Quantum Industry Summit in Glasgow last June. Another excellent turn on stage from him. Jose Pozo, CTO of Optica, put the full talk online this week.

Here is the write-up.

→ Compute moves to a 2D grid. The two qubit gate, the hardest operation in a trapped ion machine, has moved from a laser aimed down a line of ions to an RF line printed into the trap chip. More than a decade of Oxford work behind it, about 99.99% fidelity, and a trap that can be laid out as a grid on a standard semiconductor line. Lasers stay in the machine for cooling and readout.

→ The network is a loss problem with a number attached. Getting a single photon out of a single ion and into fiber costs about 20 dB, the same loss as 100 km of good fiber. It is paid at both ends, so about one attempt in 10,000 produces entanglement. Ten years of photonic link demos have run into that ratio.

→ Quantum memory is how IonQ gets around it, and IonQ has it because of Lightsynq. The diamond memory out of the company Bhaskar founded and IonQ bought last year sits between the two processors and holds a photon from one side while the other side keeps trying, so both ends stop having to land at the same moment. Around 99% storage fidelity, about 3 dB loss, over 100 MHz of bandwidth, wide enough to take photons from machines that emit at a few MHz.

→ The economics work in the data center first. Interconnect is 20 to 40% of the cost of a high performance NVIDIA cluster, which leaves room for a quantum interconnect to cost real money and still make sense.

→ Sensing is the same idea in orbit. Vector Atomic clocks and Skyloom laser terminals, bought within a year of each other, are the two halves of a timing network. That level of timing is the argument behind positioning a thousand times better than GPS.

→ The fab is about speed. SkyWater takes the design and verification loop for a new quantum chip from about 6 months to about 3 weeks. It was announced when he spoke in June, and he says so on stage. IonQ closed it six weeks later, on July 31.

→ 2028 is the date to hold him to. Logical qubits moving between processors, the point where separate machines start behaving like one data center.

Then the Q&A.

→ Chris Myatt of QPICs asked the awkward one. Why would a rival send its chip designs to a fab owned by IonQ.

→ Bhaskar went at the shared layers, the ones every platform needs and none of them wins on: interposers, packaging that mixes diamond and lithium niobate, cryogenic control chips, optical engines.

Posted by Jose Pozo, CTO of Optica. ⬇️

$IONQ IonQ ran Walking Cat's error correction on one laptop chip.

Min Ye, Andrii Maksymov and Nicolas Delfosse, arXiv, 25 August.

A quantum computer writes down its own mistakes, one page every millisecond, one per block.

Each page has to be read by an ordinary computer before the next one lands.

Fall behind and the machine stops and waits, and the wait grows on its own.

It is the same page every time, by design, which is why one reader keeps up.

That design is Walking Cat, the machine this decoder is built for.

The pages come from a simulation, and the reading was timed on a real chip.

Their conclusion: "real-time decoding is not a bottleneck at MegaQuOp scale."
